extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, publicists, communications/media-relations staff who pitch journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing email pitches to journalists that get coverage: what to include, what to avoid, and measurable constraints for subject lines, length, sourcing, and follow-up behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization to journalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Use real name, correctly spelled; reference specific recent work; tailor angle to their beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: Template not personalized. Auto-delete. Guidance emphasizes addressing the reporter by name, referencing specific recent coverage or work to show research, and tailoring the story angle to the reporter's beat to preserve relationships and increase pickup chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid template/spam pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not send generic template openings (e.g., 'Hi [FIRST NAME], I'd like to introduce you to our amazing client...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'The Spam Pitch' — templated, impersonal emails are auto-deleted. Use bespoke language and avoid obvious mail-merge phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the reporter's beat
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitch topics relevant to the reporter's beat; do not pitch mismatched topics (e.g., consumer product to enterprise reporter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: 'The Wrong Beat Pitch' shows no research and damages future relationships. Always check what the reporter covers and tailor the story accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest/accurate framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame claims honestly; do not inflate terms like 'exclusive' or 'breaking', and don't claim 'first' or call something 'revolutionary' without evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Misleading Subject Line: 'EXCLUSIVE: Major Announcement' for a routine product update erodes reporter trust. Inflated language leads to loss of credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject line must reflect content
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject line should accurately describe the pitch and not overstate importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific anti-pattern: Misleading Subject Line. Guidance elsewhere: keep subject under 60 characters (see brevity). Inflated subject lines are flagged and damage trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid buzzword-heavy language ('buzzword soup')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on generic buzzwords (e.g., 'revolutionary, game-changing, AI-powered, blockchain-enabled') in place of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: 'The Buzzword Soup' — all buzzwords and no substance leads to being filtered as spam. Provide concrete facts instead of hype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes must add information
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes should provide insight or new information, not generic PR-speak ('We are excited to bring this innovative solution to market').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: 'The PR-Speak Quote' — quotes that say nothing are useless. Use quotes to illuminate motivation, impact, or context that the rest of the pitch doesn't convey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable claims and named sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be verifiable; where research or data are cited, include methodology details and named sources with credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'The Anonymous Source' — 'According to our research...' without methodology or named source is unverified and dismissed. Include provenance, sample size, dates, or expert names to substantiate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specific numbers, not vague claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete metrics and figures instead of vague qualitative assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 'Substance Matters': reporters prefer specific numbers. Vague claims ('users love it', 'rapid growth') should be quantified to be credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity: keep it short
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the pitch concise: subject line under 60 characters; body under 200 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: 'The 1,000-Word Email' — reporters scan for news and will delete overly long messages. Short, scannable pitches perform better.

rubrics_metrics.name: One news item per pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit each pitch to a single, clear news item rather than multiple unrelated announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 'Brevity Matters': reporters expect a single news focus per pitch. Multiple items dilute the story and reduce chances of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single clear ask
rubrics_metrics.description: Include one explicit call-to-action (e.g., request an interview, offer comment, provide asset access).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality Rubric: 'Single clear ask' — pitches should make it obvious what you want the reporter to do; avoid multiple asks or vague requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: No aggressive follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repeated, pestering follow-ups (e.g., 'Just following up... And the one before...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: 'The Aggressive Follow-Up' — persistent follow-ups annoy reporters and damage relationships. Allow reasonable time and limit follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise overall framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain concise, non-promotional framing throughout the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality Rubric: 'Concise (under 200 words)' and 'Honest framing throughout' — combine brevity with honest, non-promotional language. Reporters want news, not sales copy.
